Note on the Equivalence of Costas Polynomials and Orthomorphisms

Amela Muratović-Ribić ††thanks: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Faculty of Science, University of Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Emails: amela@pmf.unsa.ba; aleksandar.bs@pmf.unsa.ba.    Aleksandar Balašev-Samarski11footnotemark: 1
June 5, 2026
Abstract

We establish an equivalence between the existence of Costas polynomials and the existence of a special kind of orthomorphism such that their compositions are also orthomorphisms. Computations are easier over these orthomorphisms. We provide a lower bound for the number of Costas polynomials and derive some of their properties. We show that Costas polynomials, by virtue of being multiplicative analogs of planar polynomials, can also be used to construct complete families of mutually orthogonal Latin squares.

Keywords: Costas polynomial; permutation polynomial; Latin square; orthomorphism

MSC 2020: 11T06; 12E20; 05B15

1 Introduction

Let pp be a prime, and q=pnq=p^{n} where nn is a positive integer. Denote by 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} the finite field of order qq. Every mapping θ\theta on 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} induces a polynomial f​(x)∈𝔽q​[x]f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x] of the degree less than qq such that θ⁡(s)=f⁡(s)\theta(s)=f(s) for all s∈𝔽q​[x]s\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]. If this mapping is a permutation of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, then we say that f⁡(x)f(x) is a permutation polynomial (PP). Polynomials of the form L⁡(x)=∑i=0n−1ai​xpiL(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_{i}x^{p^{i}} are called linearized permutation polynomials since these are linear operators of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} (see [6]).

A Costas array of order nn is a n×nn\times n permutation array (with exactly one dot in every row and column and blanks elsewhere) such that every vector connecting two dots is distinct. The Costas property ensures that the array has ideal auto-correlation, which makes Costas arrays highly desirable for use in RADAR and SONAR communications. A special case is the circular Costas sequence, which motivated the definition of Costas polynomials. For more information, see [2, 4, 5, 8, 10].

Definition 1.1.

Suppose f∈𝔽q​[x]f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x] is such that f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)f(dx)-f(x) is a permutation polynomial for all d∈𝔽qd\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, d≠1d\neq 1. Then ff is called a Costas polynomial.

Without lost of generality we can assume f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0. According to an existing conjecture (see [5]) the only circular Costas sequence is exponential Welch, or, equivalently, the only Costas polynomial over the prime field is of the form xsx^{s}, with gcd⁡(s,q−1)=1\gcd(s,q-1)=1. Known classes of Costas polynomials include f⁡(x)=xsf(x)=x^{s} where gcd⁡(q−1,s)=1\gcd(q-1,s)=1 for any field. In the case where 𝔽qm\mathbb{F}_{q^{m}} is an extension field and L⁡(x)=∑i=0nai​xqiL(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}x^{q^{i}} is a linearized permutation polynomial of 𝔽qm\mathbb{F}_{q^{m}} over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, then L⁡(xs)L(x^{s}) is also a Costas polynomial for all ss such that gcd⁡(s,qm−1)=1\gcd(s,q^{m}-1)=1. It is conjectured in [8] that these are the only Costas polynomials.

A Latin square of order nn on a set SS, where |S|=n|S|=n, is a table (matrix) of dimension n×nn\times n with elements from SS such that in each row and each column the elements are distinct. Usually SS is a finite group with nn elements and nn rows, and columns are labeled by elements of the group. Latin squares are widely used to make schedules, in design theory, etc. (see [3]) . The element in the ii-th row and the jj-th column of the Latin square ℒ\mathcal{L} is denoted by ℒi,j\mathcal{L}_{i,j}. Two Latin squares are said to be equivalent if the second Latin square can be obtained from the first by permuting the rows, columns, and elements. Two Latin squares ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒦\mathcal{K} of the same order nn are said to be mutually orthogonal if the ordered pairs (ℒi,j,𝒦i,j)(\mathcal{L}_{i,j},\mathcal{K}_{i,j}) are distinct for all 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n. The maximum number of pairwise mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order nn is n−1n-1, and they can be constructed over finite fields of order n=qn=q by ℒi,ja=i+a​j\mathcal{L}^{a}_{i,j}=i+aj where i,j∈𝔽qi,j\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, a∈𝔽q∗a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. Let f:G→Gf\colon G\rightarrow G. By Mann ([7]), the Latin squares ℒi,j=i+j\mathcal{L}_{i,j}=i+j and 𝒦i.j=i+f⁡(j)\mathcal{K}_{i.j}=i+f(j), i,j∈Gi,j\in G are mutually orthogonal if both f⁡(x)f(x) and f⁡(x)−xf(x)-x are permutations of the group GG.

Definition 1.2.

Let GG be a finite group, and θ:G→G\theta\colon G\rightarrow G. We say that θ\theta is an orthomorpism if both θ⁡(x)\theta(x) and θ⁡(x)−x\theta(x)-x are permutations on GG.

We say that f⁡(x)f(x) is an orthomorphism in a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} if it is an orthomorphism in its additive group (𝔽q,+)(\mathbb{F}_{q},+).

2 Properties of Orthomorphisms Derived from Costas Polynomials

Let f⁡(x)f(x) be a Costas polynomial over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, i.e. f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)f(dx)-f(x) are permutation polynomials (PP) for all d∈𝔽q∖{1}d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\setminus\{1\}. In particular, if d=0d=0 then it follows that f⁡(x)f(x) is a PP. Using the substitution x=f−1​(y)x=f^{-1}(y) in the expression f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)f(dx)-f(x), we obtain that f⁡(d​f−1​(y))−yf(df^{-1}(y))-y is a PP for all d∈𝔽q∖{1}d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\setminus\{1\}.

Let d∈𝔽q∗d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} and denote gd​(x)=f⁡(d​f−1​(x))g_{d}(x)=f(df^{-1}(x)). As a composition of PPs, gd​(x)g_{d}(x) is again a PP. Therefore, both gd​(x)g_{d}(x) and gd​(x)−xg_{d}(x)-x are permutations of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} and gd​(x)g_{d}(x) is an orthomorphism for d∈𝔽q∖{1}d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\setminus\{1\}. Denote by gn(x)=g∘g∘⋯∘g(x)g^{n}(x)=g\circ g\circ\cdots\circ g(x) the nn-fold composition of g⁡(x)g(x) with itself. Then gd2​(x)=f⁡(d​f−1​(f⁡(d​f−1​(x))))=f⁡(d2​f−1​(x))=gd2​(x),g_{d}^{2}(x)=f\big(df^{-1}(f(df^{-1}(x)))\big)=f(d^{2}f^{-1}(x))=g_{d^{2}}(x), and by induction it follows that gdn​(x)=gdn​(x)g_{d}^{n}(x)=g_{d^{n}}(x) is also an orthomorphism.

Theorem 2.1.

There exists a Costas polynomial f⁡(x)f(x) over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} if and only if there exists an orthomorphism g⁡(x)g(x) such that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and all of its compositions gk​(x)g^{k}(x) are also orthomorphisms for k=1,2,…,q−2k=1,2,\ldots,q-2. They are related through the relation g⁡(x)=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))g(x)=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x)), where α\alpha is a primitive element in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Moreover, all Costas polynomials are of the form L⁡(xs)L(x^{s}) where L⁡(x)L(x) is a linearized permutation and gcd⁡(s,q−1)=1\gcd(s,q-1)=1 if and only if the only orthomorphisms such that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and all its compositions gk​(x)g^{k}(x), k=1,2,…,q−2k=1,2,\ldots,q-2, are orthomorphisms of the form g⁡(x)=L⁡(α​L−1​(x))g(x)=L(\alpha L^{-1}(x)) where L⁡(x)L(x) is a linearized permutation and α\alpha is a primitive element in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Proof.

Assume f⁡(x)f(x) is a Costas polynomial and define g⁡(x)=gα​(x)=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))g(x)=g_{\alpha}(x)=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x)) where α\alpha is a primitive element in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. From f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0, it follows g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0. Then we have gk​(x)=gαk​(x)=f⁡(αk​f−1​(x))g^{k}(x)=g_{\alpha^{k}}(x)=f(\alpha^{k}f^{-1}(x)) and gk​(x)=gαk​(x)−xg^{k}(x)=g_{\alpha^{k}}(x)-x are all PPs for 1≤k≤q−21\leq k\leq q-2. Therefore, the compositions gk​(x)g^{k}(x) are orthomorphisms for all 1≤k≤q−21\leq k\leq q-2.

Conversely, assume now that there exists an orthomorphism g⁡(x)g(x) such that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and all gk​(x)g^{k}(x), 1≤k≤q−21\leq k\leq q-2, are orthomorphisms. Every orthomorphism φ\varphi has exactly one fixed point (since φ⁡(x)−x\varphi(x)-x is a PP), thus from g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 follows that 00 is the only fixed point of the permutation g⁡(x)g(x). If x0≠0x_{0}\neq 0 lies in a cycle of length t<q−1t<q-1 in the permutation g⁡(x)g(x) of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, then x0=gt​(x0)x_{0}=g^{t}(x_{0}), which implies gt​(x0)−x0=0=gt​(0)−0g^{t}(x_{0})-x_{0}=0=g^{t}(0)-0, contradicting the fact that gt​(x)−xg^{t}(x)-x is a PP. Therefore, the permutation g⁡(x)g(x) has one fixed element 00 and one cycle of length q−1q-1. Let α\alpha be a primitive element of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Then the PP h⁡(x)=α​xh(x)=\alpha x has the same cycle structure. Thus, g⁡(x)g(x) and h⁡(x)h(x) are conjugate; i.e. there exists a permutation f⁡(x)f(x) such that g=f∘h∘f−1g=f\circ h\circ f^{-1}, or equivalently g⁡(x)=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))g(x)=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x)). Using gk​(x)=f⁡(αk​f−1​(x))g^{k}(x)=f(\alpha^{k}f^{-1}(x)), 1≤k≤q−21\leq k\leq q-2, we see that f⁡(αk​f−1​(x))−xf(\alpha^{k}f^{-1}(x))-x are permutations. Substituting y=f−1​(x)y=f^{-1}(x), we obtain that f⁡(αk​y)−f⁡(y)f(\alpha^{k}y)-f(y) are all permutations for 1≤k≤q−21\leq k\leq q-2. Therefore, f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)f(dx)-f(x) are permutations for d≠1d\neq 1; i.e., f⁡(x)f(x) is a Costas polynomial.

Assume now the Costas polynomial f⁡(x)f(x) is of the form f⁡(x)=L⁡(xs)f(x)=L(x^{s}). Then gα​(x)=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))=L⁡(αs​(L−1​(x)))g_{\alpha}(x)=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x))=L(\alpha^{s}(L^{-1}(x))), which is a linearized polynomial. Conversely, assume that gα​(x)=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))g_{\alpha}(x)=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x)) is of the form L⁡(β​L−1​(x))L(\beta L^{-1}(x)) where β=αs,gcd⁡(s,q−1)=1\beta=\alpha^{s},\gcd(s,q-1)=1, T​O​D​O:βTODO:\beta is a primitive element of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, i.e. L⁡(β​L−1​(x))=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))L(\beta L^{-1}(x))=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x)). Then αs​(L−1∘f)​(y)=(L−1∘f)​(α​y)\alpha^{s}(L^{-1}\circ f)(y)=(L^{-1}\circ f)(\alpha y). Comparing the coefficients of the polynomials on both sides we conclude that L−1∘fL^{-1}\circ f is a monomial, more precisely L−1∘f⁡(y)=ysL^{-1}\circ f(y)=y^{s}. Thus f⁡(y)=L⁡(ys)f(y)=L(y^{s}). ∎

Corollary 2.1.1.

The orthomorphism g⁡(x)g(x) has one fixed point 00 and one cycle of length q−1q-1.

We now show that the orthomorphism g⁡(x)g(x) corresponds to a Costas polynomial if and only if gk​(x)g^{k}(x) corresponds to a Costas polynomial for all kk such that gcd⁡(k,q−1)=1\gcd(k,q-1)=1.

Corollary 2.1.2.

Let g⁡(x)g(x) be such that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and has one cycle of length q−1q-1. It then follows that all the compositions gs​(x),1≤s≤q−2g^{s}(x),1\leq s\leq q-2, are orthomorphisms if and only if all the ss-folded compositions gk​s​(x)g^{ks}(x) of gk​(x)g^{k}(x) with 1≤s≤q−21\leq s\leq q-2 are orthomorphisms for all kk such that gcd⁡(q−1,k)=1\gcd(q-1,k)=1. In particular, g−1​(x)g^{-1}(x) is an orthomorphism, g⁡(x)g(x) is such that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0, it has one cycle of the length q−1q-1 and all of its compositions gs​(x),1≤s≤q−2g^{s}(x),1\leq s\leq q-2 are orthomorphisms.

Proof.

From gcd⁡(q−1,k)=1\gcd(q-1,k)=1 if follows that the cycle structures of g⁡(x)g(x) and gk​(x)g^{k}(x) are the same. Moreover, since the gs​(x)g^{s}(x) are all orthomorphisms (or all are non-orthomorphisms) for s=1,2,…,q−2s=1,2,\ldots,q-2 and gq−1​(x)=id⁡(x)=xg^{q-1}(x)=\mathrm{id}(x)=x, it follows that (gk)s​(x)=gk​s​(x)=gk​s(modq−1)​(x)(g^{k})^{s}(x)=g^{ks}(x)=g^{ks\pmod{q-1}}(x) is an orthoomorphism (or is a non-orthomorphisms) for all s=1,2,…,q−2s=1,2,\ldots,q-2, and conversely. Note that g−1​(x)=gq−2​(x)g^{-1}(x)=g^{q-2}(x) As gcd⁡(q−1,q−2)=1\gcd(q-1,q-2)=1 it follows that g−1​(x)g^{-1}(x) is an orthomorphism of the given property.∎

Using the fact that L⁡(xs)L(x^{s}) is Costas, we obtain:

Corollary 2.1.3.

Let L⁡(x)L(x) be a linearized polynomial over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, and let dd be a primitive element. Then g⁡(x)=L⁡(d​L−1​(x))g(x)=L(dL^{-1}(x)) satisfies g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0. It has one cycle of length q−1q-1, and all of its compositions gk​(x)g^{k}(x), for 1≤k≤q−21\leq k\leq q-2, are orthomorphims. Moreover, gq−1​(x)=xg^{q-1}(x)=x.

Theorem 2.2.

The lower bound for the number of Costas polynomials over the field FqF_{q}, where q=pnq=p^{n}, is

φ⁡(q−1)​(q−1)​(q−p)​…​(q−pn−1)n⁡(q−1).\varphi(q-1)\frac{(q-1)(q-p)\ldots(q-p^{n-1})}{n(q-1)}.
Proof.

All orthomorphims of the form L⁡(α​L−1​(x))L(\alpha L^{-1}(x)), where α\alpha is a primitive element in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} and L⁡(x)L(x) is a linearized permutation polynomial, produce a Costas polynomial. There are φ⁡(q−1)\varphi(q-1) primitive elements in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, and there are (q−1)​(q−p)​…​(q−pn−1)(q-1)(q-p)\ldots(q-p^{n-1}) linearized permutation polynomials over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. However, L⁡(α​L−1​(x))=L1​(β​L1−1​(x))L(\alpha L^{-1}(x))=L_{1}(\beta L_{1}^{-1}(x)) is equivalent to (L1−1∘L)​(α​x)=β⁡(L1−1∘L)​(x)(L_{1}^{-1}\circ L)(\alpha x)=\beta(L_{1}^{-1}\circ L)(x). Therefore, L1−1∘L⁡(x)=a​xpjL_{1}^{-1}\circ L(x)=ax^{p^{j}} for some a∈𝔽q∗a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} and j∈{0,1,…,n−1}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}. This implies that (q−1)​n(q-1)n choices of L⁡(x)L(x) and α\alpha yield the same orthomorphism. Consequently, the number of distinct orthomorphisms (and thus Costas polynomials of this form) is φ⁡(q−1)​(q−1)​(q−p)​…​(q−pn−1)n⁡(q−1)\varphi(q-1)\frac{(q-1)(q-p)\ldots(q-p^{n-1})}{n(q-1)}, where φ⁡(n)\varphi(n) denotes the Euler totient function. ∎

Note that the same result can also be obtained by counting the L⁡(xs)L(x^{s}). We conclude from the above that the conjecture proposed in [8], namely that the only Costas polynomials are those of the form L⁡(xs)L(x^{s}), gcd⁡(q−1,s)=1\gcd(q-1,s)=1 is equivalent to the following conjecture:

Conjecture.

The only mappings g⁡(x)g(x) with fixed point 00 and a cycle of length q−1q-1, and such that all of their compositions gk​(x)g^{k}(x), 1≤k≤q−21\leq k\leq q-2 are orthomorphisms, are those of the form L⁡(α​L−1​(x))L(\alpha L^{-1}(x)) where L⁡(x)L(x) is a linearized permutation polynomial and α\alpha is a primitive element of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Computationally, it is easier to find all orthomorphisms gg, with g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and a single cycle of length q−1q-1, such that all their compositions are orthomorphisms, due to the specific cycle structure of g⁡(x)g(x), than to investigate which permutation polynomials are Costas. Note that there are (q−1)!(q-1)! permutation polynomials with fixed point 00, and one must store the full table of preimages and images to test whether a permutation is Costas. On the other hand, there are (q−2)!(q-2)! permutations gg with g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and having one cycle of length q−1q-1, and it suffices to store only the cycle. Using the fact that gk​(x),gcd⁡(k,q−1)=1g^{k}(x),\gcd(k,q-1)=1 preserves the property of being (or not being) an orthomorphism of the specified type, we need to investigate (q−2)!/φ⁡(q−1)(q-2)!/\varphi(q-1)\qquad q−1q-1-cycles to determine whether all of their compositions are orthomorphisms. Assume that for a subarray in the q−1q-1-cycle (…,ci,ci+1​…​cj+t,…)(\ldots,c_{i},c_{i+1}\ldots c_{j+t},\ldots) we establish that ci+t−ci=cj+t−cj,i≠jc_{i+t}-c_{i}=c_{j+t}-c_{j},i\neq j, i.e. that it is not an orthomorphism, then all permutations with this subarray in its q−1q-1-cycle are also non-orthomorphisms, which significantly reduces the number of computations.

3 Counting number of permutations in C++

As stated earlier, we want to find all the permutations gg of the field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} with the property g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and gg is of the form g=(c0​c1​…​cq−2)g=(c_{0}\ c_{1}\ \ldots\ c_{q-2}) with ci≠0c_{i}\neq 0 for i∈{0,…,q−2}i\in\{0,\ldots,q-2\}, (i.e. gg is a cycle of length q−1q-1 which fixes the element 00) such that g⁡(x)−xg(x)-x is a permutation. To produce all permutations g=(c0​c1​…​cq−2)g=(c_{0}\ c_{1}\ \ldots\ c_{q-2}), g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0, with the desired property, it is sufficient to generate all cycles (c0​c1​…​cq−2)(c_{0}\ c_{1}\ldots\ c_{q-2}), and to verify if g⁡(x)−xg(x)-x is injective, or equivalently, to check if c(k+j)mod(q−1)−ckc_{(k+j)\mod(q-1)}-c_{k} are all distinct, for each k∈{0,…,q−2}k\in\{0,\ldots,q-2\}, and for each iteration j∈{1,…,q−2}j\in\{1,\ldots,q-2\}. Note that we allow here for 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} to be any finite field, i.e. q=pnq=p^{n} for some prime pp and natural nn, and use natural identification between elements of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} and elements of set {0,…,q−1}\{0,\ldots,q-1\} and identification 𝔽pn=𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{p^{n}}=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}.

Obviously, we can (and will) assume c0=1c_{0}=1.

The naive algorithm for finding all such permutations would be to generate all permutations gg of the cycle (1 2​…​q−1)(1\ 2\ \ldots\ q-1), and to check whether the permutation gj−idg^{j}-\mathrm{id} is injective for all j∈{1,…,q−2}j\in\{1,\ldots,q-2\}. In that way, we obtain the complexity (q−2)!​(q−2)​(q−1)(q-2)!(q-2)(q-1). Caution should be exercised for last two terms, since we do not know how many possible (q−2)​(q−1)(q-2)(q-1) checks would be performed for each permutation.

The first optimization is to compare subarrays as mentioned above.

The second optimization is more inclined towards C++. We use bitwise ’or’ and bitwise shift operators for checking the injectivity part, and to keep information on whether the permutation so far is injective (for fixed jj), one machine word (32 bits on most modern computers) is enough to keep the information about the (partial) set of image values – instead of qq bytes or qq words. Since a rollback operation – undoing data of injectivity – can happen and happens in each level of 11 to q−2q-2, every improvement that can be done in a partial step (verifying injectivity; rolling back) of scale cc factors to up cq−2c^{q-2}.

In terms of generalization, we note that our algorithm can find the permutations for any field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, since the only specific part regarding the underlying field is the (pregenerated) table of subtraction. This has to be done only once for a target field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. As a side note, our benchmarks showed that certain (but small) speed improvements have already been achieved introducing the subtraction operation table, so it is already a welcome improvement. A number of orthomorphisms for fields of order less than 3030 are given in the table, and this matches the lower bound given in Theorem 2.2.

Thus, for q≤30q\leq 30, all Costas polynomials are of the form L⁡(xs)L(x^{s}) where LL is a linearized permutation polynomial and gcd⁡(q−1,s)=1\gcd(q-1,s)=1.

4 Some additional properties of Costas polynomials

Proposition 4.1.

Let f⁡(x)f(x) be a Costas polynomial. Let d∈𝔽q∖{1}d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\setminus\{1\} and let gd​(x)=f⁡(d​f−1​(x))g_{d}(x)=f(df^{-1}(x)). We let hd​(x)=f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)h_{d}(x)=f(dx)-f(x). Then the following holds:

  • a)

    The function hd​(x)+hd​(d​x)+⋯+hd​(ds​x)=hds+1​(x)h_{d}(x)+h_{d}(dx)+\cdots+h_{d}(d^{s}x)=h_{d^{s+1}}(x) is a permutation polynomial for all ss such that ds+1≠1d^{s+1}\neq 1. If ds+1=1d^{s+1}=1, then hd​(x)+hd​(d​x)+⋯+hd​(ds​x)=0h_{d}(x)+h_{d}(dx)+\cdots+h_{d}(d^{s}x)=0 .

  • b)

    gt∘gs=gt​sg_{t}\circ g_{s}=g_{ts}.

Proof.
  • a)

If ds+1=1d^{s+1}=1, then we have

    hd​(x)+hd​(d​x)+⋯+hd​(ds​x)=(f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x))+(f⁡(d2​x)−f⁡(d​x))+⋯+(f⁡(ds+1​x)−f⁡(ds​x)).h_{d}(x)+h_{d}(dx)+\cdots+h_{d}(d^{s}x)=\\ (f(dx)-f(x))+(f(d^{2}x)-f(dx))+\cdots+(f(d^{s+1}x)-f(d^{s}x)).

    This telescopes to =f⁡(ds+1​x)−f⁡(x)=f⁡(x)−f⁡(x)=0.=f(d^{s+1}x)-f(x)=f(x)-f(x)=0.

  • b)

∎

Proposition 4.2.

Let f⁡(x)=∑i=0q−2xif(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{q-2}x^{i} be a Costas polynomial over a field of odd characteristic. Then ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0 implies aq−1−i=0a_{q-1-i}=0 for all i=1,2,…,q−2i=1,2,\ldots,q-2.

Proof.

Let G⁡(x)=∑i=0q−1bi​xiG(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}b_{i}x^{i}. Then the coefficient of xq−1x^{q-1} in G​(x)2G(x)^{2} equals ∑i=0q−1bi​bq−1−i\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}b_{i}b_{q-1-i}. If G⁡(x)G(x) is a permutation polynomial, then by the Hermite criterion we have ∑i=0q−1bi​bq−1−i=0\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}b_{i}b_{q-1-i}=0 (see [6]). We apply this to Costas polynomials. If f⁡(x)f(x) is Costas, then f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)=∑i=0q−1ai​(di−1)​xif(dx)-f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}a_{i}(d^{i}-1)x^{i} is a permutation polynomial for all d∈𝔽q∖{1}d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\setminus\{1\}. Let G⁡(x)=[f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)]G(x)=[f(dx)-f(x)]. The coefficient with xq−1x^{q-1} in (G⁡(x))2=[f⁡(d​x)−f⁡(x)]2(G(x))^{2}=[f(dx)-f(x)]^{2} is

∑i=0q−1ai​aq−1−i​(di−1)​(dq−1−i−1).\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}a_{i}a_{q-1-i}(d^{i}-1)(d^{q-1-i}-1).

Expanding yields

∑i=0q−1ai​aq−1−i​(dq−1+1)−2​∑i=0q−1ai​aq−1−i​di=0,\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}a_{i}a_{q-1-i}(d^{q-1}+1)-2\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}a_{i}a_{q-1-i}d^{i}=0,

d≠1d\neq 1. Viewed as a polynomial in dd, this expression vanishes for all d≠1d\neq 1. Therefore, it must be either the zero polynomial or a scalar multiple of (dq−d)⋅(d−1)−1=dq−1+dq−2+⋯+d(d^{q}-d)\cdot(d-1)^{-1}=d^{q-1}+d^{q-2}+\cdots+d.

Since f⁡(x)f(x) is a permutation polynomial, we also have ∑i=0q−1ai​aq−1−i=0\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}a_{i}a_{q-1-i}=0, so the first term vanishes and we obtain

−2∑i=0q−1aiaq−1−idi=0.-2\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}a_{i}a_{q-1-i}d^{i}=0.

This implies ai​aq−1−i=0a_{i}a_{q-1-i}=0 for all ii, and hence ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0 implies aq−1−i=0a_{q-1-i}=0. ∎

Therefore, we conclude that Costas polynomials have at least half of their coefficients equal to zero.

In all cases of orthomorphisms with fixed point 00 and a single cycle of length q−1q-1, such that all of their compositions are also orthomorphisms, we have gq−12​(x)=−xg^{\frac{q-1}{2}}(x)=-x in fields of order q≤30q\leq 30. If f=L⁡(xs)f=L(x^{s}) and g⁡(x)=L⁡(αs​L−1​(x))g(x)=L(\alpha^{s}L^{-1}(x)), then gq−12​(x)=L⁡(−L−1​(x))=−L⁡(L−1​(x))=−xg^{\frac{q-1}{2}}(x)=L(-L^{-1}(x))=-L(L^{-1}(x))=-x. This motivates the following proposition.

Proposition 4.3.

For a Costas polynomial f⁡(x)f(x), the mapping g⁡(x)=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))g(x)=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x)) has the property gq−12​(x)=−xg^{\frac{q-1}{2}}(x)=-x if and only if f⁡(x)f(x) is an odd function.

Proof.

If gq−12​(x)=−xg^{\frac{q-1}{2}}(x)=-x then f⁡(−f−1​(x))=−xf(-f^{-1}(x))=-x which implies −f−1​(x)=f−1​(−x)-f^{-1}(x)=f^{-1}(-x). Let x=f⁡(y)x=f(y). Then −f−1​(f⁡(y))=f−1​(−f⁡(y))-f^{-1}(f(y))=f^{-1}(-f(y)), i.e. f−1​(−f⁡(y))=−yf^{-1}(-f(y))=-y and hence −f⁡(y)=f⁡(−y)-f(y)=f(-y). Thus, f⁡(x)f(x) is an odd function.

Conversely, if f⁡(x)f(x) is odd, then g⁡(x)=f⁡(α​f−1​(x))g(x)=f(\alpha f^{-1}(x)) is also odd (as a composition of odd functions), and all of its compositions are odd functions. In particular, gq−12​(−x)=f⁡(−f−1​(x))=−f⁡(f−1​(x))=−xg^{\frac{q-1}{2}}(-x)=f(-f^{-1}(x))=-f(f^{-1}(x))=-x. ∎

5 Construction of Latin Squares

A planar polynomial f​(x)∈𝔽q​[x]f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x] is a polynomial such that f⁡(x+a)−f⁡(x)f(x+a)-f(x) is a permutation polynomial for every a∈𝔽q∗a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. Planar polynomials cannot be bijective. It is known that if f⁡(x)f(x) is planar, then the family of Latin squares defined by ℒi​ja=i+f⁡(j+a)−f⁡(j)\mathcal{L}^{a}_{ij}=i+f(j+a)-f(j) forms a complete family of pairwise mutually orthogonal Latin squares (see [1], Theorem 5.3). Costas polynomials are the multiplicative analogue of planar polynomials.

Theorem 5.1.

Let f​(x)∈𝔽q​[x]f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x] be a Costas polynomial. Then the family of Latin squares defined by

ℒi,jd=i+f⁡(d​j)−f⁡(j),d≠1\mathcal{L}^{d}_{i,j}=i+f(dj)-f(j),\quad d\neq 1

is a complete family of pairwise mutually orthogonal Latin squares.

Proof.

Note first that there are q−1q-1 of such Latin squares. We compare ordered pairs of elements in the Latin squares ℒd\mathcal{L}^{d} and ℒs\mathcal{L}^{s} where d≠s,d,s≠1d\neq s,d,s\neq 1. Assume

(i+f⁡(d​j)−f⁡(j),i+f⁡(s​j)−f⁡(j))=(k+f⁡(d​t)−f⁡(t),k+f⁡(s​t)−f⁡(t)),i,j,k,t∈𝔽q.(i+f(dj)-f(j),i+f(sj)-f(j))=(k+f(dt)-f(t),k+f(st)-f(t)),i,j,k,t\in\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Then subtracting the equalities

i+f⁡(d​j)−f⁡(j)=k+f⁡(d​t)−f⁡(t)i+f(dj)-f(j)=k+f(dt)-f(t)

and

i+f⁡(s​j)−f⁡(j)=k+f⁡(s​t)−f⁡(t)i+f(sj)-f(j)=k+f(st)-f(t)

we obtain

f⁡(d​j)−f⁡(s​j)=f⁡(d​t)−f⁡(s​t).f(dj)-f(sj)=f(dt)-f(st).

Using the substitutions z=s​j,y=s​tz=sj,y=st we obtain f⁡(d​s−1​z)−f⁡(z)=f⁡(d​s−1​y)−f⁡(y)f(ds^{-1}z)-f(z)=f(ds^{-1}y)-f(y). The polynomial f⁡(d​s−1​x)−f⁡(x)f(ds^{-1}x)-f(x) is a permutation polynomial, and thus z=yz=y which implies j=tj=t and, consequently, i=ki=k. Therefore, ℒd\mathcal{L}^{d} and ℒs\mathcal{L}^{s} are mutually orthogonal. ∎

The function gα​(x)=L⁡(α​L−1​(x))g_{\alpha}(x)=L(\alpha L^{-1}(x)), which is obtained from known Costas polynomials, is a strong complete mapping and can be used to construct Knut Vik designs and complete families of MOLS (see [9]).

Furthermore, on the multiplicative group 𝔽q∗\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}, the orthomorphism f⁡(d​f−1​(x))=ℒx,df(df^{-1}(x))=\mathcal{L}_{x,d}, where f⁡(x)f(x) is a Costas polynomial, defines a Latin square (d=yd=y) where rows and columns are denoted by x,d∈𝔽q∗x,d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. This Latin square is equivalent to the known Latin square Kx,y=x​yK_{x,y}=xy. On the other hand, if the rows are labeled by d∈𝔽q∖{1}d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\setminus\{1\} and the columns by x∈𝔽q∗x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}, then we can also obtain the Latin square ℒd,x=f⁡(d​f−1​(x))−x\mathcal{L}_{d,x}=f(df^{-1}(x))-x of order q−1q-1 with elements in 𝔽q∗\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}.

Code availability

The implementation used in this paper is publicly available at https://github.com/samarski/costas. A permanent archived version corresponding to this manuscript is available through Zenodo at DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20549103.
